description: Grishneshwar, also spelled Ghrishneshwar, is a Shiva temple in the village of Verul, close to the Ellora caves in Maharashtra. Devotees count it among the twelve Jyotirlingas, and traditional lists place it last. The building is in the Hemadpanthi style, with a large Nandi figure in front of the sanctum entrance. Historical accounts describe damage during the medieval period, rebuilding in the 16th century by Maloji Bhosale, grandfather of Shivaji, and a later restoration in the 18th century linked to the Holkar family of Indore. Mahashivratri is the principal festival.

description: Bhimashankar is a Shiva temple in the Bhimashankar forest range of Pune district, Maharashtra, counted by devotees among the twelve Jyotirlingas. According to tradition, the name recalls Shiva's conflict with the demon Tripurasura, and the Bhima river is said to rise here; the trust's account places the start of its eastward flow at Kusharanya tirtha near the temple. The temple is described as Nagara in style, with a separate Nandi shrine close by. Texts mention the shrine from about the 13th century, the sabhamandap is credited to Nana Phadnavis in the 18th century, and a bell offered by Chimaji Appa, taken from Vasai Fort after a victory over the Portuguese, hangs here. Mahashivratri is especially important, and sacred pools nearby add to the pilgrimage.

description: Tulja Bhavani Temple at Tuljapur, in Dharashiv (formerly Osmanabad) district, is dedicated to Bhavani, regarded as a form of Durga and revered as the family goddess of many Maratha clans. It stands on a hill in the Balaghat range. According to tradition recorded in the Skanda Purana, the goddess took birth to kill the demon Kukur, who disturbed the penance of the widow Anubhuti, and then stayed on this hill at her request. The complex is built of dark stone in the Hemadpanthi style, and devotees bathe in the Gomukh and Kallol tanks before entering the sanctum. The temple trust, registered in 1962, runs a daily cycle of abhishek and aarti. Pilgrims gather in large numbers at festival times such as Navaratri, and on special occasions the image is carried in procession through the town.

description: The Mahalaxmi Temple, also called the Ambabai Temple, stands in the Karveer area of Kolhapur and is dedicated to Mahalakshmi, who is worshipped here as the city's principal goddess. Shakta tradition counts it among the three and a half Shakti Peethas. The crowned four-armed image, described by the Ministry of Culture's Utsav portal as made of a gemstone and weighing about 40 kg, holds a citron, mace, shield and drinking bowl, with a lion standing behind her. Unusually, the image faces west. The stone structure is described as Hemadpanthi in style, and its carvings suggest an origin in the Chalukya period, roughly the 7th century, though the date is not firmly established. Festivals observed here include Navratri, Kirnotsav and Rathotsav.

description: The Kalika Mata, or Mahakali, Temple crowns Pavagadh hill in Panchmahal district, close to the Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The sanctum houses the red-painted head of Kalika Mata, a full image of Mahakali and yantras of Bahucharamata. According to tradition, the toe of Sati fell here, making it one of the Shakti Peethas. Sources place the shrine around the 10th to 11th centuries, and a redevelopment inaugurated in June 2022 gave it a new spire and a restored flagpole, with the original sanctum kept intact. Pilgrims either climb the footpath and renovated steps from Manchi or take the ropeway.

description: The Ranchhodraiji Temple at Dakor in Kheda district is dedicated to Ranchhodrai, a four-armed form of Vishnu worshipped here in a youthful Krishna aspect. According to tradition, the cowherd-devotee Bodana brought the image from Dwarka, and the Dwarka priests who followed him were told to pay the image's weight in gold. The temple's own history page records that in 1769 the villages of Dakor and Kanjari were granted by the Peshwa and the Gaekwad of Baroda for the deity's upkeep; the present building dates from 1772. The shrine stands on a raised plinth with brick walls, stone pillars, domes and turrets, and a drummers' gallery over the main gate. Devotees come throughout the year, with larger gatherings on full-moon days, and a Friday procession links the temple to the separate Lakshmiji temple.

description: The Bahucharaji temple at Becharaji in Mehsana district is dedicated to Bahuchara Mata, a form of the Mother Goddess worshipped here as Bala. Gujarat Tourism describes it as one of the state's three Shakti Peethas, alongside Ambaji and Pavagadh, while the central government's Utsav portal places it among the 52 Shakti Peethas. The goddess is regarded as a protector of women, who pray to her for relief from domestic and family troubles, and the temple is also a major pilgrimage site for the transgender community. The present stone temple is attributed to Manajirao Gaekwad of Baroda, built in the late 18th century (the year 1839 given on the Utsav portal corresponds to Samvat 1839, about 1783 CE). Devotees come to offer vows and seek blessings, with a folk fair held on Chaitra Purnima, and the Shree Bahucharaji Mataji Temple Trust organises events.

description: The Sun Temple at Modhera, on the Pushpavati river in Mehsana district, was dedicated to Surya and is a protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India. It dates to the Solanki (Chaulukya) period; Gujarat Tourism, citing ASI, gives 1026-27 CE in the reign of Bhima I. Facing east in Maru-Gurjara style, it has a sanctum and closed hall, a detached pillared assembly hall with carvings of the twelve Adityas, and a large stepped tank, the Suryakund, lined with 108 small shrines. The original sun image and the tower above the sanctum no longer survive. Worship no longer takes place in the sanctum, so it is visited as a heritage monument rather than an active place of worship. Gujarat Tourism notes that at the equinox sunlight is said to light the inner sanctum.

description: The Karni Mata Temple at Deshnoke, about 30 km from Bikaner, honours Karni Mata, a medieval Charan ascetic whom devotees regard as an incarnation of Durga and whom the rulers of Bikaner treated as their family deity. According to tradition, she advised the founders of Jodhpur and Bikaner and laid the foundation stones of their forts. The present complex grew in phases around a small original shrine. Rajasthan government sources credit Maharaja Surat Singh with the enclosure wall and entrance gate, and Maharaja Ganga Singh with the form seen today, including its silver doors. The temple is best known for the many rats, called kabas, which devotees consider sacred and which must not be harmed. Fairs are held during both Navratri periods, and Mangla aarti begins the daily worship.

description: The Brahma Temple in Pushkar, beside the sacred Pushkar Lake in Ajmer district, is dedicated to Brahma, the creator in the Hindu triad, and is one of the few temples dedicated to him. The sanctum holds a four-faced image of Brahma, with Gayatri also enshrined. According to tradition, the sage Vishwamitra founded it after a yajna and Adi Shankaracharya later renovated it. The Rajasthan Devasthan Department gives about 1401 CE for the present structure, while the Archaeological Survey of India records repeated repairs, the latest in 1809. It is built of marble and stone slabs joined with molten lead, on a raised platform with a red spire, and devotees have set inscribed silver coins into its floor. Pilgrims bathe in the lake first; the Kartik fair and lunar-phase rites draw crowds.

description: Salasar Balaji in Churu district is a Hanuman temple on the Jaipur-Bikaner highway and one of Rajasthan's major Hanuman pilgrimage centres. Its image of Hanuman is distinctive for a round face with a moustache and beard. According to tradition, a farmer ploughing near Asota unearthed the idol, and a devotee named Mohandas, guided by dreams, had it installed at Salasar. Devotees offer savamani food of dal, bati and churma, Sunderkand is recited on Tuesdays, and many pilgrims arrive on foot. A trust manages the temple, and large fairs are held on Chaitra Purnima and Sharad Purnima.
